Deleting every ε-production of the grammar.
Deleting useless symbols, that is, non-generating and unreachable symbols.
Reordering the alternatives of a non-LL(1) grammar until it becomes LL(1).
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A transformation is language-preserving when the set of terminal strings derivable from the start symbol is unchanged. Left-recursion elimination and left factoring are such transformations; deleting ε-productions and reordering alternatives are not, in general.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true: A → A α | β generates β αk for k ≥ 0, and so does A → β A′ with A′ → α A′ | ε.
  2. (B) true: factoring only regroups alternatives, it derives exactly the same strings.
  3. (C) false: dropping every ε-production removes ε from the language and breaks every derivation that relied on an optional part; a correct elimination must add compensating productions instead of merely deleting.
  4. (D) true: a symbol that generates no terminal string, or that can never be reached from the start symbol, contributes nothing to the language.
  5. (E) false: reordering alternatives cannot remove a FIRST/FIRST or FIRST/FOLLOW conflict; the ambiguity stays in the grammar. Only rewriting the rules helps.

Answer: options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing every "clean-up" step is safe. ε-elimination is language-preserving only when it is done properly — replicating the nullable symbols into the other right sides — and even then ε is lost unless the start symbol is nullable.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: A predictive parser uses the grammar E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → ( E ) | id. For the input id + id it applies a sequence of productions. How many productions are applied in total, counting each ε-production that is applied? (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: A predictive parser uses the grammar E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → ( E ) | id. For the input id + id it applies a sequence of productions. How many productions are applied in total, counting each ε-production that is applied? (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A predictive parser expands nonterminals left to right, and each expansion is the application of exactly one production. The count is therefore the number of nonterminal expansions in the leftmost derivation of the input, including the expansions of the ′-nonterminals to ε.

Step by step.

  1. E → T E′ — 1.
  2. T → F T′ — 2.
  3. F → id, matching the first id — 3.
  4. T′ → ε, since the lookahead is + and + ∈ FOLLOW(T′) — 4.
  5. E′ → + T E′, consuming the + — 5.
  6. T → F T′ — 6.
  7. F → id, matching the second id — 7.
  8. T′ → ε, lookahead $ — 8.
  9. E′ → ε, lookahead $ — 9.

Answer: 9 productions.

Common misconception. Counting only the "visible" productions and dropping the two ε-expansions. Every nonterminal in the sentential form must be expanded, and a nonterminal that disappears by ε still costs one production.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: A grammar is LL(1) if and only if, for every pair of distinct alternatives α and β of a nonterminal A,
questions.question_html: A grammar is LL(1) if and only if, for every pair of distinct alternatives α and β of a nonterminal A,
options: FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅, and if α ⇒* ε then FIRST(β) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ (and symmetrically for β).
FIRST(α) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ for both alternatives.
FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅ and FOLLOW(A) = ∅.
the grammar contains no ε-production.
options_html: FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅, and if α ⇒* ε then FIRST(β) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ (and symmetrically for β).
FIRST(α) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ for both alternatives.
FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅ and FOLLOW(A) = ∅.
the grammar contains no ε-production.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The LL(1) condition is exactly the statement that no cell of the parsing table receives two entries. Two ways of colliding are possible: two alternatives can start with the same terminal, or a nullable alternative can vanish on a terminal that another alternative can start with.

Step by step.

  1. FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅ rules out the first kind of collision: no terminal selects two alternatives by starting them.
  2. If α ⇒* ε, then A → α is entered in every cell M[A, b] with b ∈ FOLLOW(A), so FIRST(β) must avoid FOLLOW(A).
  3. Options B and C are too strong: FOLLOW(A) may be non-empty, it just must not overlap the FIRST sets of the other alternatives.
  4. Option D is false: S → a S b | ε contains an ε-production and is LL(1).

Answer: option A.

Common misconception. Thinking LL(1) forbids ε-productions. It only requires that the ε-alternative be distinguishable from the others by the lookahead, which is what the FOLLOW test checks.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A B, A → ε | a, B → b | ε, the set FIRST(B) is
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A B, A → ε | a, B → b | ε, the set FIRST(B) is
options: {b, ε}
{ε}
{a, b, ε}
options_html: {b}
{b, ε}
{ε}
{a, b, ε}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST of a nonterminal is the union of the FIRST sets of its alternatives, taken one production at a time.

Step by step.

  1. B → b contributes b.
  2. B → ε contributes ε.
  3. No other production has B on the left.
  4. Hence FIRST(B) = {b, ε}.

Answer: {b, ε} — option B.

Common misconception. Reading the alternatives of A into FIRST(B), or writing {ε} alone because B is nullable. Nullability adds ε; it does not remove the terminals.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following statements about recursive-descent parsing are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about recursive-descent parsing are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Without memoisation, a backtracking recursive-descent parser can take time exponential in the input length on some grammars.
For an LL(1) grammar one token of lookahead always selects the alternative, so no backtracking is needed.
Recursive descent handles a left-recursive grammar directly, because the recursion in the parser mirrors the recursion in the grammar.
Left recursion must be removed before a recursive-descent parser is written.
A recursive-descent parser builds the parse tree bottom-up, from the leaves to the root.
options_html: Without memoisation, a backtracking recursive-descent parser can take time exponential in the input length on some grammars.
For an LL(1) grammar one token of lookahead always selects the alternative, so no backtracking is needed.
Recursive descent handles a left-recursive grammar directly, because the recursion in the parser mirrors the recursion in the grammar.
Left recursion must be removed before a recursive-descent parser is written.
A recursive-descent parser builds the parse tree bottom-up, from the leaves to the root.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A recursive-descent parser has one procedure per nonterminal, and a procedure calls the procedures of the symbols on the right side of the alternative it chooses. It is therefore a top-down, leftmost-derivation parser, and its control flow copies the shape of the grammar.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true: with backtracking, each failed alternative may re-parse the same suffix, and the number of partial parses can grow exponentially — the classical reason backtracking descent is avoided in production compilers.
  2. (B) true: LL(1) means the parsing table has at most one entry per cell, and a recursive-descent parser implements that table directly.
  3. (C) false: for A → A α | β the procedure for A calls itself before consuming any input, so it recurses forever without making progress.
  4. (D) true: that is why the elimination of Unit-2 left-recursion removal precedes the parser construction.
  5. (E) false: bottom-up parsing (shift-reduce) builds the tree from the leaves; recursive descent builds it from the root downwards.

Answer: options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming the parser's recursion can "handle" the grammar's recursion. The parser mirrors the grammar, so a left-recursive rule becomes an infinite loop rather than a left-associative parse.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: In the grammar F → ( E ) | id, how many terminals belong to FIRST(F)? (Enter an integer. Do not count ε, since F is not nullable.)
questions.question_html: In the grammar F → ( E ) | id, how many terminals belong to FIRST(F)? (Enter an integer. Do not count ε, since F is not nullable.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST(F) is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from F.

Step by step.

  1. F → ( E ) begins with the terminal (.
  2. F → id begins with the terminal id.
  3. Neither alternative is nullable, so ε ∉ FIRST(F).
  4. Hence FIRST(F) = {(, id} — two terminals.

Answer: 2 terminals.

Common misconception. Counting ) or E. ) comes after E and never begins a string of F, and E is a nonterminal, not a terminal.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A a | b, A → S d | c, indirect left recursion is removed by substituting the S-productions into A and then removing the immediate left recursion. The resulting productions for A are
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A a | b, A → S d | c, indirect left recursion is removed by substituting the S-productions into A and then removing the immediate left recursion. The resulting productions for A are
options: A → A a d | b d | c, with no further step needed
A → b d A′ | c A′, A′ → a d A′ | ε
A → b d | c, A′ → a d A′
A → S d | c, unchanged, because the recursion is in S
options_html: A → A a d | b d | c, with no further step needed
A → b d A′ | c A′, A′ → a d A′ | ε
A → b d | c, A′ → a d A′
A → S d | c, unchanged, because the recursion is in S
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Indirect (mutual) left recursion is removed in two stages: substitute the earlier nonterminal's alternatives into the later one, which turns the indirect recursion into an immediate one, and then apply the standard immediate-elimination rule.

Step by step.

  1. Take the order S then A. In A → S d, replace S by its alternatives: A → A a d | b d, together with the existing A → c.
  2. Now A is immediately left recursive with α = a d and β ∈ {b d, c}.
  3. Apply the rule: A → b d A′ | c A′ and A′ → a d A′ | ε.
  4. S itself is not left recursive and stays as it is.

Answer: A → b d A′ | c A′, A′ → a d A′ | ε — option B.

Common misconception. Stopping after the substitution (option A) — the grammar is then still left recursive, only immediately so — or forgetting that the substituted alternative b d also needs the A′ suffix.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about FIRST and FOLLOW sets is FALSE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about FIRST and FOLLOW sets is FALSE?
options: FOLLOW(A) can contain $ only if A can occur as the rightmost symbol of a sentential form.
If A is nullable and occurs at the end of a production, then FOLLOW(A) contains the FOLLOW of the head of that production.
FIRST(A) contains ε exactly when A is nullable.
FOLLOW(A) contains ε whenever A is nullable.
options_html: FOLLOW(A) can contain $ only if A can occur as the rightmost symbol of a sentential form.
If A is nullable and occurs at the end of a production, then FOLLOW(A) contains the FOLLOW of the head of that production.
FIRST(A) contains ε exactly when A is nullable.
FOLLOW(A) contains ε whenever A is nullable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST describes what a string can begin with, and ε is a legitimate "beginning" of a nullable string. FOLLOW describes what can come after a nonterminal in a sentential form; its symbols are always terminals or the end marker $, never ε.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true: $ enters FOLLOW(A) only through the propagation rule for a symbol at the right end of a production, which ultimately traces back to S.
  2. (B) true: this is the standard propagation rule, including the chain through nullable symbols.
  3. (C) true: it is the definition of nullability expressed through FIRST.
  4. (D) false: FOLLOW(A) is a set of terminals and $. Nullability puts ε in FIRST(A) and is handled in the table by copying the ε-production across FOLLOW(A), not by putting ε inside it.

Answer: option D is false.

Common misconception. Symmetry. FIRST and FOLLOW look similar but are asymmetric: FIRST may hold ε, FOLLOW never does; FOLLOW holds $, FIRST never does.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following grammars are LL(1)? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following grammars are LL(1)? (Select all that apply.)
options: S → a S b | ε
S → A a | b, A → b | ε
S → a A | b B, A → c | ε, B → c | ε
E → E + T | T
S → i E t S S′ | a, S′ → e S | ε, E → b
options_html: S → a S b | ε
S → A a | b, A → b | ε
S → a A | b B, A → c | ε, B → c | ε
E → E + T | T
S → i E t S S′ | a, S′ → e S | ε, E → b
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Test each nonterminal: the FIRST sets of its alternatives must be disjoint, and where an alternative is nullable its FOLLOW set must not overlap the FIRST sets of the others. A grammar is LL(1) only if every nonterminal passes.

Step by step.

  1. S → a S b | ε: FIRST sets are {a} and {ε}; FOLLOW(S) = {b, $} does not contain a. LL(1).
  2. S → A a | b with A → b | ε: FIRST(A a) = {b, a} because A can be b or ε, and FIRST(b) = {b}. Both contain b, so M[S, b] gets two entries. Not LL(1).
  3. S → a A | b B, A → c | ε, B → c | ε: FOLLOW(A) = FOLLOW(B) = {$}, so M[A, c] = A → c, M[A, $] = A → ε and likewise for B. The two nonterminals never share a row, so no conflict. LL(1).
  4. E → E + T | T is left recursive: the two alternatives of E have the same FIRST set. Not LL(1).
  5. The dangling-else grammar has two entries in M[S′, e]. Not LL(1).

Answer: options (A) and (C).

Common misconception. Judging by the look of the rules. Option C looks suspicious because A and B have identical right sides, yet it is LL(1): conflicts are per row of the table, and A and B occupy different rows.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A B C, A → a | ε, B → b | ε, C → c | ε, how many symbols does FOLLOW(A) contain? Count $ as a symbol. (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A B C, A → a | ε, B → b | ε, C → c | ε, how many symbols does FOLLOW(A) contain? Count $ as a symbol. (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. When A is followed by a string of nullable symbols, every terminal that can begin one of them follows A, and if all of them can vanish, the FOLLOW of the head propagates as well.

Step by step.

  1. A occurs in S → A B C, followed by B C.
  2. FIRST(B) − {ε} = {b}, so b ∈ FOLLOW(A).
  3. B is nullable, so FIRST(C) − {ε} = {c} also enters: c ∈ FOLLOW(A).
  4. C is nullable too, so the rest of the right side can vanish completely and FOLLOW(S) = {$} propagates: $ ∈ FOLLOW(A).
  5. FOLLOW(A) = {b, c, $}, three symbols.

Answer: 3 symbols.

Common misconception. Answering 2 by stopping at B, or answering 4 by counting ε. Nullability is what carries the FOLLOW of the head into FOLLOW(A), and ε is never a member of a FOLLOW set.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: In a table-driven predictive parser the symbol on top of the stack is the nonterminal A, the current input symbol is a, and M[A, a] = A → X Y Z. The parser
questions.question_html: In a table-driven predictive parser the symbol on top of the stack is the nonterminal A, the current input symbol is a, and M[A, a] = A → X Y Z. The parser
options: pops A and pushes Z, then Y, then X, so that X is on top.
pops a from the input and pushes A.
shifts a onto the stack.
reduces the handle X Y Z to A.
options_html: pops A and pushes Z, then Y, then X, so that X is on top.
pops a from the input and pushes A.
shifts a onto the stack.
reduces the handle X Y Z to A.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A predictive parser keeps a stack of grammar symbols with the start symbol at the bottom. When the top is a nonterminal it expands it using the table; when the top is a terminal it must match the current input symbol and is popped.

Step by step.

  1. The stack is … A with A on top, so A is popped.
  2. The right side X Y Z is pushed in reverse order — Z first, then Y, then X — so that X, the leftmost symbol, ends up on top and is matched next.
  3. Nothing is consumed from the input at this step; the input pointer moves only when a terminal on top matches.
  4. Options B, C and D describe shift-reduce (bottom-up) behaviour, not predictive parsing.

Answer: option A.

Common misconception. Pushing the right side left to right. That would put Z on top and the parser would try to match the rightmost symbol first — a rightmost, not leftmost, derivation.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: A backtracking recursive-descent parser is used on a grammar with no LL(1) guarantee. In the worst case, for an input of length n, the work it may do grows
questions.question_html: A backtracking recursive-descent parser is used on a grammar with no LL(1) guarantee. In the worst case, for an input of length n, the work it may do grows
options: linearly in n
as n log n
exponentially in n
as n²
options_html: linearly in n
as n log n
exponentially in n
as n²
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A predictive (LL(1)) parser is linear because the table fixes every decision. A backtracking parser instead explores alternatives, and when several alternatives can match the same prefix the number of partial parses can double with every token.

Step by step.

  1. On failure the parser restores the input position and tries the next alternative, re-parsing the same suffix.
  2. If the grammar allows k alternatives at each of n levels, the search tree has on the order of kn nodes.
  3. Classic examples, such as the ambiguous expression grammar, show this exponential blow-up in practice.
  4. Memoisation (packrat parsing) removes the repetition and restores linear time at the cost of memory — but that is no longer plain backtracking.

Answer: exponentially in n — option C.

Common misconception. Assuming any parser is linear in the input. Linearity is a property of the deterministic table-driven method, not of top-down parsing in general.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following statements about left recursion and left factoring are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about left recursion and left factoring are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Left factoring can turn a grammar that is not LL(1) into an LL(1) grammar without changing the language.
Removing left recursion always yields an LL(1) grammar.
Indirect left recursion must be removed by substituting in a fixed order of nonterminals before the immediate left recursion is removed.
A recursive-descent parser that meets a left-recursive alternative recurses forever.
Left factoring introduces no new nonterminals.
options_html: Left factoring can turn a grammar that is not LL(1) into an LL(1) grammar without changing the language.
Removing left recursion always yields an LL(1) grammar.
Indirect left recursion must be removed by substituting in a fixed order of nonterminals before the immediate left recursion is removed.
A recursive-descent parser that meets a left-recursive alternative recurses forever.
Left factoring introduces no new nonterminals.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Left recursion and FIRST/FIRST conflicts are the two obstacles to predictive parsing. Left-recursion elimination removes the first; left factoring removes the second. Neither is a complete LL(1) transformation by itself.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true: a grammar whose only defect is a shared prefix becomes LL(1) after factoring, and factoring preserves the language.
  2. (B) false: S → a A | b B, A → c | ε, B → c | ε is free of left recursion and is LL(1) — but S → A a | b, A → b | ε is also free of left recursion and is not LL(1), because of a FIRST/FIRST conflict.
  3. (C) true: the substitution step turns mutual recursion into immediate recursion, and it needs a fixed order (for example A1, …, An) or the process does not terminate.
  4. (D) true: the procedure for A calls itself before consuming input.
  5. (E) false: factoring creates a new nonterminal (here A′) for every common prefix it extracts.

Answer: options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing "no left recursion" implies "LL(1)". FIRST/FIRST and FIRST/FOLLOW conflicts survive left-recursion removal untouched.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A a | b, A → b | ε, which statement about its LL(1) parsing table is TRUE?
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A a | b, A → b | ε, which statement about its LL(1) parsing table is TRUE?
options: Exactly one cell, M[S, b], holds two entries, so the grammar is not LL(1).
The grammar is LL(1), because the two alternatives of A begin differently.
M[A, a] holds A → b.
M[A, $] holds A → ε.
options_html: Exactly one cell, M[S, b], holds two entries, so the grammar is not LL(1).
The grammar is LL(1), because the two alternatives of A begin differently.
M[A, a] holds A → b.
M[A, $] holds A → ε.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The FIRST set of a right side is computed left to right, and a nullable first symbol lets the following symbols contribute. It is FIRST(A a), not FIRST(A), that decides the row of S.

Step by step.

  1. FIRST(A) = {b, ε}, so FIRST(A a) = {b} ∪ {a} = {b, a}: A may be b, or it may vanish and let a begin the string.
  2. FIRST(b) = {b}, so M[S, b] receives both S → A a and S → b. That is the conflict.
  3. FOLLOW(A) = {a}, so M[A, b] = A → b and M[A, a] = A → ε; M[A, $] stays empty.
  4. So options C and D name cells that hold the wrong entry, and option B ignores the conflict in row S.

Answer: M[S, b] holds two entries — option A.

Common misconception. Checking only the alternatives of the "suspicious" nonterminal A. Here A is perfectly well behaved; the conflict is created one level up, by the nullability of A inside S → A a.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following is true of every top-down parser?
questions.question_html: Which of the following is true of every top-down parser?
options: It builds a leftmost derivation of the input string.
It builds a rightmost derivation in reverse.
It reduces handles at the top of the stack.
It can parse every context-free grammar.
options_html: It builds a leftmost derivation of the input string.
It builds a rightmost derivation in reverse.
It reduces handles at the top of the stack.
It can parse every context-free grammar.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A top-down parser starts at the start symbol and expands nonterminals until the frontier matches the input. Expanding the leftmost nonterminal at every step produces a leftmost derivation, so the parse tree grows from the root towards the leaves.

Step by step.

  1. Recursive descent and LL(1) table-driven parsing both expand the leftmost nonterminal, giving a leftmost derivation — statement A.
  2. Statement B describes bottom-up (shift-reduce) parsing, which reconstructs a rightmost derivation in reverse.
  3. Statement C is the handle-reduction step of LR parsing, again bottom-up.
  4. Statement D is false: a top-down parser needs a grammar free of left recursion and FIRST/FIRST conflicts; many context-free grammars, including all ambiguous ones, are outside its reach.

Answer: option A.

Common misconception. Confusing "top-down" with "backtracking" or with "handles". Top-down means root-to-leaves and leftmost expansion; handles and rightmost derivations belong to the bottom-up family.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Consider the grammar S → A b, A → c | ε. Which one of the following is FIRST(S)?
questions.question_html: Consider the grammar S → A b, A → c | ε. Which one of the following is FIRST(S)?
options: {c, b}
{c, b, ε}
options_html: {c}
{c, b}
{c, b, ε}
{b}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST of a string is read left to right: the first symbol contributes its own FIRST set without ε, and only when that symbol is nullable does the next symbol contribute.

Step by step.

  1. FIRST(A) = {c, ε}, because the alternative c gives the terminal c and the alternative ε makes A nullable.
  2. In S → A b, A comes first, so c ∈ FIRST(S); ε itself never enters FIRST(S).
  3. Because A is nullable, the scan moves on to b, so b ∈ FIRST(S).
  4. S itself derives no empty string, so ε is not in FIRST(S). Hence FIRST(S) = {c, b}.

Answer: {c, b} — option (B).

Common misconception. Writing {c, b, ε} because A is nullable. ε belongs to FIRST(A), not to FIRST(S); a nullable symbol passes the scan to the next symbol, it does not pass ε along.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: In a table-driven predictive parser the symbol on top of the stack is a terminal that equals the current input symbol. The parser must
questions.question_html: In a table-driven predictive parser the symbol on top of the stack is a terminal that equals the current input symbol. The parser must
options: replace the stack top by the right side of a production.
pop the terminal from the stack and advance the input to the next symbol.
report a syntax error, because a terminal can never reach the top of the stack.
push the current input symbol onto the stack and continue.
options_html: replace the stack top by the right side of a production.
pop the terminal from the stack and advance the input to the next symbol.
report a syntax error, because a terminal can never reach the top of the stack.
push the current input symbol onto the stack and continue.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The parser has three actions only: expand a nonterminal using the table, match a terminal against the input, and report an error. A match consumes one symbol from each side.

Step by step.

  1. The stack top is a terminal and the input symbol equals it, so the two agree on the next symbol of the sentential form.
  2. The parser pops that terminal from the stack and advances the input pointer past the matching symbol.
  3. No production is applied: expansions are only triggered when the stack top is a nonterminal.

Answer: Pop the stack top and advance the input — option (B).

Common misconception. Choosing to expand a production here. The table M[A, a] is consulted only when the stack top A is a nonterminal; a terminal on top is matched, never expanded.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → a A | B c, A → b | ε, B → d, how many terminals belong to FIRST(S)? Do not count ε, since S is not nullable. (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → a A | B c, A → b | ε, B → d, how many terminals belong to FIRST(S)? Do not count ε, since S is not nullable. (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST of a nonterminal is the union of the FIRST sets of its alternatives, and a nullable symbol that ends an alternative adds nothing to that alternative's FIRST set.

Step by step.

  1. FIRST(A) = {b, ε} and FIRST(B) = {d}.
  2. Alternative a A: it begins with the terminal a, so a is in FIRST(S); A is nullable but it is the last symbol, so the scan ends there and contributes no further terminal.
  3. Alternative B c: B contributes d, so d ∈ FIRST(S).
  4. S is not nullable, so ε is excluded: FIRST(S) = {a, d}, two terminals.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Counting three terminals, by imagining that the nullable A at the end of a A lets the scan reach some further symbol. There is no symbol after A, so the scan stops.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: The grammar A → x y z | x y w | x v is left factored as far as possible. Which one of the following is the result?
questions.question_html: The grammar A → x y z | x y w | x v is left factored as far as possible. Which one of the following is the result?
options: A → x A′; A′ → y z | y w | v
A → x A′; A′ → y A″ | v; A″ → z | w
A → x A′; A′ → y A″ | v A‴; A″ → z | w
A → A′ x; A′ → y z | y w | v
options_html: A → x A′; A′ → y z | y w | v
A → x A′; A′ → y A″ | v; A″ → z | w
A → x A′; A′ → y A″ | v A‴; A″ → z | w
A → A′ x; A′ → y z | y w | v
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Left factoring removes the longest common prefix of two or more alternatives and repeats on the remainder until no two alternatives of a nonterminal share a first symbol.

Step by step.

  1. All three alternatives begin with x, so A → x A′ with A′ → y z | y w | v.
  2. Two alternatives of A′ still share the prefix y, so factor again: A′ → y A″ | v.
  3. The remainder z | w has no common prefix: A″ → z | w.
  4. Factoring stops here because every nonterminal now has alternatives with distinct first symbols.

Answer: Option (B) — A → x A′; A′ → y A″ | v; A″ → z | w.

Common misconception. Stopping after one factoring step, which leaves A′ → y z | y w with the shared prefix y still in place, so FIRST sets of two alternatives still overlap.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following statements about an LL(1) parsing table are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about an LL(1) parsing table are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A cell of the table may hold more than one production when the grammar is not LL(1).
If a nonterminal A is nullable, the FOLLOW set of A decides which columns of row A receive A → ε.
A nullable nonterminal contributes entries only in the columns of its own FIRST set.
In the table of an LL(1) grammar no cell can hold two different productions.
Deleting every ε-production from a grammar leaves its parsing table unchanged.
options_html: A cell of the table may hold more than one production when the grammar is not LL(1).
If a nonterminal A is nullable, the FOLLOW set of A decides which columns of row A receive A → ε.
A nullable nonterminal contributes entries only in the columns of its own FIRST set.
In the table of an LL(1) grammar no cell can hold two different productions.
Deleting every ε-production from a grammar leaves its parsing table unchanged.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The table is filled by two rules: A → α goes into M[A, a] for each a ∈ FIRST(α), and A → ε goes into M[A, b] for each b ∈ FOLLOW(A). A grammar is LL(1) exactly when no cell receives two entries.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: when two rules place different productions in one cell, that cell holds both, and the grammar is not LL(1).
  2. (B) True: A → ε can be applied only when the lookahead can follow A, which is precisely FOLLOW(A).
  3. (C) False: A → ε is placed using FOLLOW, not FIRST, so a nullable nonterminal also writes into columns outside its FIRST set.
  4. (D) True: that is the definition of LL(1) — a single entry per cell gives the parser a unique move for every lookahead.
  5. (E) False: ε-productions create the FOLLOW-driven entries, so deleting them removes cells and changes the language.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing that a nullable nonterminal writes only into its FIRST columns. The ε-alternative is entered through FOLLOW, which is how a predictive parser knows the nonterminal may vanish here.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → a A | b, A → c | ε, which cell of the LL(1) parsing table holds the production A → ε?
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → a A | b, A → c | ε, which cell of the LL(1) parsing table holds the production A → ε?
options: M[A, c]
M[A, b]
options_html: M[A, c]
M[A, b]
M[A, $]
M[S, $]
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A production A → ε is entered in the columns given by FOLLOW(A): the parser may drop A exactly when the next input symbol is one that can legitimately follow A.

Step by step.

  1. FOLLOW(A) = FOLLOW(S) = {$}, because A appears only at the end of S → a A.
  2. So A → ε goes into M[A, $].
  3. The alternative A → c occupies M[A, c] instead, so no cell receives two entries and the grammar is LL(1).

Answer: M[A, $] — option (C).

Common misconception. Entering A → ε in M[A, c]. The column is the lookahead token that triggers the move, and ε is applied when the lookahead follows A, not when it starts A.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Immediate left recursion is removed from every nonterminal of the grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → ( E ) | id. How many productions does the resulting grammar contain in total? (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: Immediate left recursion is removed from every nonterminal of the grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → ( E ) | id. How many productions does the resulting grammar contain in total? (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The rewrite for A → A α₁ | … | A αₘ | β₁ | … | βₙ is A → β₁ A′ | … | βₙ A′ together with A′ → α₁ A′ | … | αₘ A′ | ε: n productions for A, m + 1 for the new nonterminal.

Step by step.

  1. E has one β (namely T) and one α (+ T): E → T E′ and E′ → + T E′ | ε — 3 productions.
  2. T has one β (F) and one α (* F): T → F T′ and T′ → * F T′ | ε — 3 productions.
  3. F has no left recursion: F → ( E ) | id stays at 2 productions.
  4. Total 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 productions.

Answer: 8

Common misconception. Answering 6 by forgetting the new nonterminals, or 12 by counting each α-alternative as an extra production of A rather than of A′.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: A recursive-descent procedure is written for the alternative A → a B c. It has matched a, called the procedure for B, and that call has returned successfully. What must it do next?
questions.question_html: A recursive-descent procedure is written for the alternative A → a B c. It has matched a, called the procedure for B, and that call has returned successfully. What must it do next?
options: match the token c and advance the input past it.
call the procedure for A again, since A appears on the left side.
push B onto an explicit stack.
reduce a B c to A and return without reading further input.
options_html: match the token c and advance the input past it.
call the procedure for A again, since A appears on the left side.
push B onto an explicit stack.
reduce a B c to A and return without reading further input.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A procedure for A walks the right side of its chosen production from left to right: a terminal is matched against the input, a nonterminal becomes a recursive call.

Step by step.

  1. The right side is a B c. The first symbol a was matched, and B was handled by its own procedure.
  2. The next symbol is the terminal c, so the procedure matches c against the current input symbol and advances.
  3. After the whole right side is consumed the procedure returns, and its caller continues with the symbol after A.

Answer: Match the terminal c and advance — option (A).

Common misconception. Expecting a recursive call for c. Only nonterminals have procedures; terminals are matched directly by consuming the input token.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following statements about FIRST and FOLLOW sets are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about FIRST and FOLLOW sets are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If A ⇒* ε, then ε ∈ FIRST(A).
If A is nullable, then FIRST(A B) = FIRST(A) ∪ FIRST(B) with ε removed from the result unless B is also nullable.
If A is not nullable, FOLLOW(A) may still contain ε.
For every nonterminal X of an LL(1) grammar, FIRST(X) ∩ FOLLOW(X) = ∅.
For the start symbol S, $ ∈ FOLLOW(S).
options_html: If A ⇒* ε, then ε ∈ FIRST(A).
If A is nullable, then FIRST(A B) = FIRST(A) ∪ FIRST(B) with ε removed from the result unless B is also nullable.
If A is not nullable, FOLLOW(A) may still contain ε.
For every nonterminal X of an LL(1) grammar, FIRST(X) ∩ FOLLOW(X) = ∅.
For the start symbol S, $ ∈ FOLLOW(S).
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST is about what a string can begin with, FOLLOW about what can come immediately after a nonterminal. ε is a FIRST symbol only; FOLLOW holds terminals and the end marker $ and never ε.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: A derives the empty string exactly when ε is in FIRST(A).
  2. (B) True: a nullable A lets the scan reach B, so B contributes its FIRST set, and the concatenation is nullable only if B is nullable too.
  3. (C) False: ε is never a member of any FOLLOW set; FOLLOW answers "which terminals may follow", and the empty string is not a terminal.
  4. (D) False: nothing forbids a terminal from both starting X and following X — the grammar S → a S | a has a in both FIRST(S) and FOLLOW(S) and is still LL(1).
  5. (E) True: the end marker is placed in FOLLOW(S) as the initialisation step of every FOLLOW computation.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (E).

Common misconception. Putting ε into a FOLLOW set when a nonterminal is nullable. FOLLOW is a set of terminals plus $; nullability affects which symbols are added, not whether ε is added.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: In an LL(1) parsing table, the rows are indexed by ______ and the columns by ______.
questions.question_html: In an LL(1) parsing table, the rows are indexed by ______ and the columns by ______.
options: terminals; nonterminals
nonterminals; terminals together with $
productions; input symbols
nonterminals; productions
options_html: terminals; nonterminals
nonterminals; terminals together with $
productions; input symbols
nonterminals; productions
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The table answers one question: given the nonterminal on top of the stack and the current input symbol, which production should be applied?

Step by step.

  1. The parser looks up M[A, a] where A is the nonterminal on top of the stack.
  2. So rows are nonterminals and columns are the lookahead symbols — the terminals of the grammar plus the end marker $.
  3. Each entry is either empty (a syntax error) or a single production, which is what makes the parse deterministic.

Answer: Rows: nonterminals; columns: terminals plus $ — option (B).

Common misconception. Swapping the two axes. The row is the symbol being expanded, the column is the token being looked at.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → a S | b, which one of the following is FOLLOW(S)?
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → a S | b, which one of the following is FOLLOW(S)?
options: {a, b}
options_html: {a}
{b}
{$}
{a, b}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FOLLOW(S) starts with $, and grows only when S appears somewhere other than at the end of a right side.

Step by step.

  1. Initialise FOLLOW(S) = {$} because S is the start symbol.
  2. In S → a S the recursive S is the last symbol, so nothing new is added beyond FOLLOW(S) itself.
  3. In S → b there is no S at all.
  4. Hence FOLLOW(S) = {$}: nothing can follow a complete sentence.

Answer: {$} — option (C).

Common misconception. Adding b to FOLLOW because b ends a production. What matters is what follows S, and here S only ever appears at the very end of a right side.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A B | c, A → a | ε, B → b, how many cells of the LL(1) parsing table are non-empty? Count a cell once however many entries it holds. (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A B | c, A → a | ε, B → b, how many cells of the LL(1) parsing table are non-empty? Count a cell once however many entries it holds. (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every production writes into one cell per symbol of its FIRST set, and an ε-production writes into one cell per symbol of FOLLOW. Rows that exist are only those of nonterminals that actually own productions.

Step by step.

  1. FIRST(A) = {a, ε}, FOLLOW(A) = FIRST(B) = {b}, FOLLOW(B) = FOLLOW(S) = {$}.
  2. Row S: S → A B covers a (from A) and b (A nullable, so B contributes); S → c covers c — three cells.
  3. Row A: A → a covers a; A → ε covers the column b from FOLLOW(A) — two cells.
  4. Row B: B → b covers b — one cell.
  5. No cell receives two entries, so the grammar is LL(1) and the total is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

Answer: 6

Common misconception. Answering 5 by stopping the row of S after the terminal a, forgetting that a nullable A lets the same production also cover the column b.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: In a predictive parser the stack top is the nonterminal A, the input symbol is a, and M[A, a] is empty. The parser must
questions.question_html: In a predictive parser the stack top is the nonterminal A, the input symbol is a, and M[A, a] is empty. The parser must
options: pop A and continue with the next symbol on the stack.
skip the input symbol a and try the next one.
report a syntax error.
apply the production A → ε.
options_html: pop A and continue with the next symbol on the stack.
skip the input symbol a and try the next one.
report a syntax error.
apply the production A → ε.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An empty cell means no production of A can start with the lookahead a and A cannot vanish here either; the input is not a sentence of the grammar.

Step by step.

  1. The table holds a production in M[A, a] exactly when A can legitimately produce something beginning with a.
  2. The cell is empty, so no legal move exists at this point of the derivation.
  3. A predictive parser has no backtracking to fall back on, so it stops and reports a syntax error.

Answer: Report a syntax error — option (C).

Common misconception. Applying A → ε. That production is legal only when the lookahead lies in FOLLOW(A), which is exactly the condition under which the cell would not be empty.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A B C, A → a, B → b, C → ε | c, which one of the following is FOLLOW(B)?
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A B C, A → a, B → b, C → ε | c, which one of the following is FOLLOW(B)?
options: {b, c}
options_html: {c}
{c, $}
{b, c}
{$}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. When B is followed by C in a right side, FOLLOW(B) takes FIRST(C) without ε, and if C is nullable it also takes FOLLOW of the left-side nonterminal.

Step by step.

  1. FIRST(C) = {c, ε}, because C → ε makes C nullable.
  2. B is followed by C in S → A B C, so c ∈ FOLLOW(B).
  3. C is nullable, so the scan runs past C to the end of the production, and FOLLOW(S) = {$} is added as well.
  4. Hence FOLLOW(B) = {c, $}.

Answer: {c, $} — option (B).

Common misconception. Answering {c} by treating C as non-nullable. Because C can vanish, whatever follows S can also follow B.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the two preprocessing rewrites — eliminating left recursion and left factoring — are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the two preprocessing rewrites — eliminating left recursion and left factoring — are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: After immediate left recursion is removed from A → A α | β, no production of A begins with A.
Left factoring never changes the language generated by the grammar.
Removing indirect left recursion is enough to make any grammar LL(1).
Left factoring always removes every LL(1) conflict a grammar has.
A left-recursive grammar can be ambiguous.
options_html: After immediate left recursion is removed from A → A α | β, no production of A begins with A.
Left factoring never changes the language generated by the grammar.
Removing indirect left recursion is enough to make any grammar LL(1).
Left factoring always removes every LL(1) conflict a grammar has.
A left-recursive grammar can be ambiguous.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Both transformations are language-preserving rewrites. Removing left recursion clears one obstacle to predictive parsing; left factoring clears another; neither is sufficient on its own.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: the result is A → β A′ with A′ → α A′ | ε, and β does not begin with A by assumption, so no production of A starts with A.
  2. (B) True: factoring only regroups alternatives under a new nonterminal, so the set of derived strings is unchanged.
  3. (C) False: a grammar can be free of left recursion and still be non-LL(1), for instance when two alternatives share a common prefix or when FIRST/FOLLOW overlap at a nullable alternative.
  4. (D) False: left factoring removes conflicts caused by a shared prefix only; conflicts from nullable alternatives, or from a grammar that is inherently ambiguous, survive it.
  5. (E) True: E → E + E | E * E | id is left recursive and ambiguous, since id + id * id has two parse trees.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (E).

Common misconception. Treating the two rewrites as a cure for every LL(1) conflict. They are necessary repairs for two specific causes of conflict, not a guarantee of LL(1)-ness.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → X Y Z, X → x | ε, Y → y | ε, Z → z | ε, how many symbols does FOLLOW(Y) contain? Count $ as a symbol. (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → X Y Z, X → x | ε, Y → y | ε, Z → z | ε, how many symbols does FOLLOW(Y) contain? Count $ as a symbol. (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FOLLOW of a symbol in the middle of a right side takes the FIRST set of everything to its right, and continues past any nullable suffix into FOLLOW of the left-side nonterminal.

Step by step.

  1. Y is followed by Z, so FIRST(Z) = {z, ε} contributes z.
  2. Z is nullable, so the scan reaches the end of S → X Y Z and adds FOLLOW(S) = {$}.
  3. ε is never a member of a FOLLOW set, so it is not counted.
  4. FOLLOW(Y) = {z, $}, two symbols.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Counting ε as a third symbol, or stopping at z without noting that the nullable Z exposes the end of the sentence.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: In a recursive-descent parser, the recursion of the host language replaces which component of a table-driven predictive parser?
questions.question_html: In a recursive-descent parser, the recursion of the host language replaces which component of a table-driven predictive parser?
options: the input buffer
the explicit parse stack
the parsing table
the output stream
options_html: the input buffer
the explicit parse stack
the parsing table
the output stream
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Both parsers are predictive and consult the same FIRST/FOLLOW information; they differ only in how the pending sentential form is held.

Step by step.

  1. A table-driven parser keeps the pending symbols on an explicit stack.
  2. A recursive-descent parser keeps them implicitly: each pending nonterminal is an active procedure call, and the call stack records the symbols still to be matched.
  3. The production to apply is still chosen by the same FIRST/FOLLOW test, so the table is not what the recursion replaces.

Answer: The explicit parse stack — option (B).

Common misconception. Saying the recursion replaces the parsing table. The choice of alternative is still driven by FIRST/FOLLOW; only the storage of the pending form moves to the call stack.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: For the grammar S → A B | B a, A → a | ε, B → b | ε, which one of the following is FOLLOW(B)?
questions.question_html: For the grammar S → A B | B a, A → a | ε, B → b | ε, which one of the following is FOLLOW(B)?
options_html: {$}
{a, $}
{a, b, $}
{b, $}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A nonterminal that occurs twice in the grammar collects contributions from every occurrence, so each occurrence must be examined separately.

Step by step.

  1. First occurrence, S → A B: B is last, so FOLLOW(S) = {$} is added.
  2. Second occurrence, S → B a: B is followed by the terminal a, so a is added.
  3. A being nullable does not matter here: A appears only in the first alternative, where it precedes B rather than following it.
  4. Hence FOLLOW(B) = {a, $}.

Answer: {a, $} — option (B).

Common misconception. Answering {$} from the first occurrence only. Every occurrence of the nonterminal contributes to its FOLLOW set.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which of the following statements about recursive-descent and predictive parsing are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about recursive-descent and predictive parsing are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A table-driven predictive parser keeps an explicit stack in place of the procedure calls of a recursive-descent parser.
A recursive-descent parser for an LL(1) grammar needs no backtracking.
The parse tree built by a top-down parser corresponds to a rightmost derivation.
The procedure for a nonterminal returns after consuming exactly the input derived from that nonterminal.
A hand-written recursive-descent parser for an LL(1) grammar may still need more than one token of lookahead.
options_html: A table-driven predictive parser keeps an explicit stack in place of the procedure calls of a recursive-descent parser.
A recursive-descent parser for an LL(1) grammar needs no backtracking.
The parse tree built by a top-down parser corresponds to a rightmost derivation.
The procedure for a nonterminal returns after consuming exactly the input derived from that nonterminal.
A hand-written recursive-descent parser for an LL(1) grammar may still need more than one token of lookahead.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A top-down parser builds a leftmost derivation: it expands the leftmost nonterminal first, and the frontier of the tree always matches the input read so far.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: the two parsers are the same algorithm with the pending sentential form stored differently — on an explicit stack or on the call stack.
  2. (B) True: the FIRST/FOLLOW test picks a unique production for each lookahead, so no alternative ever has to be undone.
  3. (C) False: top-down parsing expands the leftmost nonterminal first, giving a leftmost derivation; a rightmost derivation in reverse is what a bottom-up parser builds.
  4. (D) True: that is the contract of the procedure — it consumes exactly the string derived from its nonterminal and leaves the rest of the input untouched.
  5. (E) False: for an LL(1) grammar one token of lookahead always determines the choice, which is what the "1" in LL(1) asserts.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing a top-down parser produces a rightmost derivation. Leftmost expansion is the definition of top-down; the reverse of a rightmost derivation is the bottom-up (shift-reduce) order.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Immediate left recursion is removed from A → A a b | A c | d. Which one of the following is the result?
questions.question_html: Immediate left recursion is removed from A → A a b | A c | d. Which one of the following is the result?
options: A → d A′; A′ → a b A′ | c A′ | ε
A → d A′; A′ → a A′ | b A′ | c A′ | ε
A → A′ d; A′ → a b A′ | c A′ | ε
A → d A′; A′ → b a A′ | c A′ | ε
options_html: A → d A′; A′ → a b A′ | c A′ | ε
A → d A′; A′ → a A′ | b A′ | c A′ | ε
A → A′ d; A′ → a b A′ | c A′ | ε
A → d A′; A′ → b a A′ | c A′ | ε
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With A → A α₁ | … | A αₘ | β, the rewrite is A → β A′ and A′ → α₁ A′ | … | αₘ A′ | ε, keeping each α intact as a whole string.

Step by step.

  1. The two recursive alternatives give α₁ = a b and α₂ = c; the non-recursive alternative gives β = d.
  2. So A → d A′.
  3. And A′ → a b A′ | c A′ | ε, with the two symbols of α₁ kept together and in order.
  4. A now generates d (ab | c)*, the same language as before.

Answer: Option (A) — A → d A′; A′ → a b A′ | c A′ | ε.

Common misconception. Splitting the multi-symbol α into separate alternatives, as option (B) does. The α must be carried across as one string; splitting it changes the language.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: The left-recursive grammar S → S a | b generates which language?
questions.question_html: The left-recursive grammar S → S a | b generates which language?
options: b a*
a* b
(a b)*
b* a
options_html: b a*
a* b
(a b)*
b* a
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Reading the grammar semantically: the only way to stop the recursion is the base alternative b, and each recursive step appends one a to the right.

Step by step.

  1. Every derivation must begin with the base case: S ⇒ b.
  2. Each application of S → S a appends a single a at the right end.
  3. So the strings are b, b a, b a a, …, that is b a*.
  4. Left recursion changes how the strings are derived, not which strings exist.

Answer: b a* — option (A).

Common misconception. Reading the recursion as prefixing, giving a* b. The recursion S → S a puts the new a on the right of what S already produced.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Consider A → B a | c, B → A b | d. Indirect left recursion is removed by substituting the A-productions into B and then removing the immediate left recursion that results. Which one of the following describes the outcome?
questions.question_html: Consider A → B a | c, B → A b | d. Indirect left recursion is removed by substituting the A-productions into B and then removing the immediate left recursion that results. Which one of the following describes the outcome?
options: B → B a b | c b | d, with no further step needed
B → c b B′ | d B′; B′ → a b B′ | ε, with A → B a | c unchanged
B → a b B′ | d B′, B′ → c b B′ | ε, with A → B a | c unchanged
B → c b | d; B′ → a b B′, with A → B a | c unchanged
options_html: B → B a b | c b | d, with no further step needed
B → c b B′ | d B′; B′ → a b B′ | ε, with A → B a | c unchanged
B → a b B′ | d B′, B′ → c b B′ | ε, with A → B a | c unchanged
B → c b | d; B′ → a b B′, with A → B a | c unchanged
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Indirect recursion is removed in two steps: substitute so the recursion becomes immediate, then apply the immediate-left-recursion rewrite.

Step by step.

  1. Substitute A → B a | c into B → A b | d: B → B a b | c b | d.
  2. This is immediate left recursion with α = a b and β ∈ {c b, d}.
  3. Rewrite: B → c b B′ | d B′ and B′ → a b B′ | ε.
  4. A keeps its productions A → B a | c, which no longer involve a cycle through B.

Answer: Option (B) — B → c b B′ | d B′; B′ → a b B′ | ε, A unchanged.

Common misconception. Stopping after the substitution, as option (A) does. Substitution only exposes the left recursion; the rewrite still has to be applied to remove it.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: A predictive parser uses E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → ( E ) | id. For the input ( id ), how many productions are applied in total, counting each application separately? (Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html: A predictive parser uses E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → ( E ) | id. For the input ( id ), how many productions are applied in total, counting each application separately? (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every nonterminal expansion costs one production application, including each ε-production used to close off E′ or T′. Terminals are matched, not expanded, so they cost nothing.

Step by step.

  1. E → T E′ (1), T → F T′ (2), F → ( E ) (3) — the opening parenthesis is matched.
  2. Inside the parentheses: E → T E′ (4), T → F T′ (5), F → id (6).
  3. T′ sees ), not *, so T′ → ε (7); E′ sees ), not +, so E′ → ε (8); the closing parenthesis is matched.
  4. Back in the outer T: T′ → ε (9) on the lookahead $; then E′ → ε (10).
  5. Total 10 productions; the two parentheses and the identifier are matched, not expanded.

Answer: 10

Common misconception. Answering 6 by counting only the productions that add terminals. Each ε-production is a real expansion and costs one application.

questions.subject: compiler-design
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about LL(1) grammars is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about LL(1) grammars is TRUE?
options: LL(1)-ness is a property of the language, so every grammar for an LL(1) language is LL(1).
LL(1)-ness is a property of the grammar, and a grammar that is not LL(1) may still generate a language that has an LL(1) grammar.
Every unambiguous grammar is LL(1).
Every deterministic context-free language has an LL(1) grammar.
options_html: LL(1)-ness is a property of the language, so every grammar for an LL(1) language is LL(1).
LL(1)-ness is a property of the grammar, and a grammar that is not LL(1) may still generate a language that has an LL(1) grammar.
Every unambiguous grammar is LL(1).
Every deterministic context-free language has an LL(1) grammar.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. LL(1) is a property of a grammar — it is decided by inspecting FIRST and FOLLOW sets of productions — while the language is the set of strings the grammar generates.

Step by step.

  1. The LL(1) test is applied to productions and their FIRST/FOLLOW sets, so it classifies grammars, not languages.
  2. The same language can have several grammars: the left-recursive E → E + T | T is not LL(1), yet the factored version E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε generates the same language and is LL(1).
  3. (C) is false: S → a S a | a is unambiguous but not LL(1), because both alternatives put a in FIRST.
  4. (D) is false: deterministic context-free languages need not be LL(1); {aⁿ bⁿ} ∪ {aⁿ cⁿ} is deterministic but has no LL(1) grammar.

Answer: Option (B) — LL(1)-ness belongs to the grammar, not the language.

Common misconception. Assuming that rewriting a language into a nicer grammar always rescues LL(1)-ness. Some deterministic languages have no LL(1) grammar at all, so the property is not a property of the language.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about FIRST and FOLLOW sets are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about FIRST and FOLLOW sets are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: For a terminal a, FIRST(a) = {a}.
The FOLLOW set of the start symbol always contains $.
If a nonterminal other than the start symbol never occurs on the right side of any production, its FOLLOW set is empty.
A FOLLOW set may contain a nonterminal as a member.
FIRST of a string is decided by its leftmost symbol alone, even when that symbol is a nullable nonterminal.
options_html: For a terminal a, FIRST(a) = {a}.
The FOLLOW set of the start symbol always contains $.
If a nonterminal other than the start symbol never occurs on the right side of any production, its FOLLOW set is empty.
A FOLLOW set may contain a nonterminal as a member.
FIRST of a string is decided by its leftmost symbol alone, even when that symbol is a nullable nonterminal.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIRST sets describe what a string can begin with; FOLLOW sets describe which terminals may appear immediately after a nonterminal, plus the end marker $ for the start symbol.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: a terminal derives only itself, so its FIRST set is the singleton {a}.
  2. (B) True: every FOLLOW computation is initialised with FOLLOW(S) = {$}.
  3. (C) True: FOLLOW of a nonterminal grows only from occurrences on right sides, so a nonterminal with no such occurrence keeps the empty set — only the start symbol is seeded with $.
  4. (D) False: FOLLOW holds terminals and $ only; a nonterminal on the right side is followed by whatever its own FOLLOW is, not by the nonterminal itself.
  5. (E) False: when the leftmost symbol is nullable, the scan continues to the next symbol, so the FIRST set of the whole string can include symbols that the leftmost symbol cannot start.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Stopping the FIRST computation at the leftmost symbol even when it is nullable, and imagining that nonterminals can appear inside FOLLOW sets.
